She had a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus, obesity, hyperthyroidism, and pernicious anemia. On questioning, the patient had been experiencing gradual onset of stiffness, rigidity, and pain in her axial muscles for 9 years, eventually leading to the inability to assume a sitting posture. She also reported episodic muscle spasms of the limbs that were triggered by sound stimulation.

extractions.value: She had a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus, obesity, hyperthyroidism, and pernicious anemia. On questioning, the patient had been experiencing gradual onset of stiffness, rigidity, and pain in her axial muscles for 9 years, eventually leading to the inability to assume a sitting posture. She also reported episodic muscle spasms of the limbs that were triggered by sound stimulation. The persistent nature of her symptoms led to pronounced lumbar lordosis. Functional consequences were pronounced with repeated falls, fractures, and loss of autonomy. During the past 6 months, she developed more frequent self-limiting acute episodes of dyspnea with cyanosis, lasting between 5 and 45 min, associated with hypertonic stiffness of axial muscles.

extractions.value: Diagnosis of SPS was suggested on clinical presentation and confirmed by an electromyographic study revealing continuous motor-unit activity and the presence of high titer of circulating antiGAD antibodies ( >1500 U/mL, N < 1 U/mL), with antiGAD65 (79 U, N < 5) specificity. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging, electroencephalography, and analysis of cerebrospinal fluid were normal. She was immunized against tetanus. Symptomatic treatment was initiated with benzodiazepine (midazolam 10 mg/h continuous intravenous infusion) and baclofen. Despite adequate sedation, management of airway pressures was difficult due to persistent episodes of axial muscle stiffness and required the use of neuromuscular blocking agents. The patient was not, however, hypoxemic and was ventilated in assist-control mode with an inspired oxygen fraction of 30 %. Symptomatic treatment was intensified with a high dose of diazepam (10 mg/h continuous infusion), and intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) (2 g/kg over 5 days) were started 3 days after admission. Following IVIG therapy, we observed a rapid clinical improvement with the disappearance of muscle stiffness and apnea, allowing the reduction of diazepam doses.
